en: Took a drum in his hands,
And beat it with a booming sound.
Of Bukhara's twelve gates,
When they heard the booming sound,
All the khans were thrown into turmoil;
All the people ran.
Bukhara's eighty wrestlers
Before Temir Khan,
Running around from every side,
All arrived.
What could poor Temir do?
"My son will go to his people;
He will reach the place he longs for.
From the royal treasury,
From the multitude of people,
A thousand winged steeds in the stables,
With Aktulpar at their head,
Drive them here.
Let us parade them in a long procession;
Let us select the finest steed.
Among those winged steeds,
Let the famed Aktulpar be included.
Here is Ysmayyl's Chongkashka,
Shaatemir's Chongkurong,
Koloy's thoroughbred Karakashka,
Agynai's Tuuchunak.
Drive the winged steeds here.
Let them parade in a procession," he said.
"Semetey and Sary Khan,
Let them take whichever they choose."
After Temir Khan gave the order,
Of the royal treasury's strongmen,
A thousand strongmen made ready.
They gathered around a thousand steeds,
Holding them short and taking the direct way.
A thousand steeds, a thousand strongmen
Bustled about leading them.
The streets filled with crowds;
Those who saw were amazed.
The city filled with crowds;
Those who watched were amazed.
The royal treasury's thousand strongmen,
Each with one animal,
Made them rear and strain,
The desolate winged steeds,
Tugging as though their riders had died.
Hurrying all the strongmen,
Pressing close upon their heels,
He set them filing past.
Kanykei and Sary Khan
Became the judges of the horses.
The steeds went past in high spirits;
How could those two approve them?
When they looked at some,
They were Karabair racing horses.
When they looked at some,
They had sieve-like lungs and copper wings.
When they looked at some,
They had camel forelocks and a pounding gait.
When they looked at some,
They were thick-limbed, with a jolting trot.
When they looked at some,
They had wild-ass rumps and owl-like feet.
When they looked at some,
They were Karabairs with a hard, restless gait.
Half the steeds had passed now,
And many strongmen had gone by.
Standing there, Kanykei came upon
Koloy Khan's Karakashka thoroughbred,
With a sparse tail and little mane,
Well accustomed to fighting foes,
High-backed, yet low of stature,
Who let no wild ass escape pursuit.
That wretched woman Kanykei,
Who had ridden often as a girl,
And fought against many enemies,
Was exceptionally skilled with a spear.
The thoroughbred Karakashka—
Kanykei chose him for herself.
‘How clear-sighted she is!’
All Bukhara marveled.
The horse judges of Bukhara
Were judging your sister-in-law,
Your mother Kanykei.
‘This woman's night must be the Night of Power;
A saint among women,
A bondwoman endowed with sacred grace.
For one who will not open his heart,
Such a soul is not to be found.
Above her right shoulder
Is the naked child Khyzyr.
Manas, who took her as his wife—
What regret could he have?’
While Bukhara was saying this,
Of the strongmen leading horses,
When five hundred had passed,
And five hundred had now arrived—
When he had settled in the forest,
When he had earned an ill name,
Quenching charcoal, black with soot,
And holding much woodland,
When he lived in degradation,
Taking charcoal and giving much away,
When his fortunes were low,
Suffering much abuse in the forest,
When his fortunes were low,
With wretched rawhide shoes upon his feet,
Looking at his household,
He had lived in poverty.
Agynai's Tuuchunak—
He knew him for a peerless steed,
And saying, ‘If he were my horse,’
He had long wished for him.
Tuuchunak's nature was like this:
Entering a tumult, he never panicked,
Nor ever put a foot amiss.
When shouting and commotion arose,
He did not panic and bellow.
When bullets struck like falling rain,
He never set a foot astray.
Hearing the tumult, he grew spirited,
Showing the qualities of a peerless steed.
If a six-day desert lay ahead,
And he were given his head,
Before one could utter a word,
In the blink of an eye,
He left the many steeds behind.
His rib bones stood out,
The mighty animal loomed tall,
Showing his supernatural nature.
If there were a dug-out trench,
Or a seething salt marsh,
He never plunged his feet in embers.
That creature Tuuchunak
Never faltered to a halt.
Unless his tether were reduced to a handspan,
He would not yield to a determined foe.
Unless a thousand disasters struck,
He would not let a foe come near.
With a sparse tail and little mane,
A swift beast akin to a whirlwind.
Entering the desert, he never weakened;
Sent over hills, he never tired.
Upon ridges of imposing height,
He never suffered the slightest saddle sore.
Though he ran for months and years,
He never tired in the end,
And never had enough of running.
No four-footed animal
Could escape when he pursued it wearily.
His crooked little ears stood up;
He did not stand out among the horses.
Ridden into battle, he did not falter;
Ridden into a lance fight, he did not bend.
Then Sary Khan said,
‘A steed as precious as life itself,’
And took hold of Tuuchunak.
Temir Khan spread out his palms,
Giving his blessing without stint.
Of the thoroughbred and Tuuchunak,
Unable to say, ‘I will not give them,’
He did not disappoint the warrior,
And showed his own generosity.
From inside the treasury,
He brought out a blue armored coat,
And clothed Sary Khan in it.
Temir Khan's Bozkelte
He now hung upon Sary Khan.
Ysmayyl's Arkesken,
Which was exceptionally sharp,
He now hung upon Sary Khan.
The exceptional orphan rejoiced;
Sary Khan's spirits were diverted,
His eyes opened wide,
His burning heart grew calm.
The watching Bukharans grieved.
If you looked at Sary Khan,
The marks of a khan were plain.
What would your poor uncle Sary do?
Thick-armed and stone-hearted,
Unless these things were presented to him,
He would bring great havoc on Bukhara.
His eyes stood out from his brow,
His heroic nature showed.
Looking him straight in the face,
No mortal could endure his presence.
If he faced them, extending his spear,
No mortal could approach him.
He was a support to rely upon;
For this orphan Semetey,
He was a binding about the waist,
A hero on whom to set one's hopes.
Then this only son of Manas,
Taking courage in ‘my uncle Sary,’
Made the bald charcoal burner a hero,
Did away with the name ‘Sary Taz,’
Made him a renowned khan,
And raised Sary Taz's fortunes.
‘While this dear head of mine is safe,
I shall stir up trouble in the world,’ he said,
Setting a golden crown upon him,
And seating him upon a golden throne,
‘If he lives, over the Argyn
I shall raise him as khan,’ he said.
Tuuchunak, whom no bullet could catch,
He gave Sary Khan to ride.
The costly blue armored coat
He had put upon him as well.
Bozkelte, adept at shooting,
He had hung upon your uncle Sary.
In your uncle Sary's hands
Were weapons of every kind.
The marks of a khan were unmistakable—
The sight diverted one's heart;
The marks of a khan appeared,
Much of his misfortune was cut away,
His thoughts were fully unburdened.
Entering Bukhara, he obtained a horse,
And himself was named ‘Sary Khan.’
Let us leave him like this,
And take up the other side.
Then Temir Khan proclaimed a decree,
To all the people without exception,
He called, ‘Let them come here!’
Temir Khan had a golden throne,
And fortune surpassing other men's.
He had executioners in plenty,
And all his strongmen were there.
Among those strongmen
Were elders who could find wise counsel.
Guarding the entrance to the gate,
His sentries were there as well.
To those sentries
No one would come near.
Human noses and ears
They wore as amulets.
People wandered clear of them;
Those who met them stood amazed.
Temir Khan ruled over all,
A man of formidable spiritual power.
Those who grappled with him lay still;
He was a khan rich in wisdom.
He had his dutars brought out,
And rattles made of iron
All played in proper rhythm.
He made his trumpets blare,
And had his booming drums struck.
He gathered his people,
And had great counsel taken.
At the golden tower,
He gathered all the people at its foot.
Roaring in his wrath,
Temir Khan proclaimed a decree:
‘Let your dignitaries come, your khans come,
Come, all you people gathered here!
Let the resourceful and skillful come,
